summary: This document updates RFC 7030 (Enrollment over Secure Transport) to clarify how an EST server can use the CSR Attributes response to specify both attribute OIDs and values, such as X.509 extension values, that it wants in a certificate request. It also updates RFC 9148.

eli5.summary: A form from the certificate office can say what to fill in and also give sample values. This clears up how that form works.

questions: what is the est csr attributes response
how does an est server specify subjectaltname
what is a csr template in est
subtitle: How an EST server can tell a client exactly which fields and values its certificate request must contain.

tldr.problem: RFC 7030 lets an EST server send CSR Attributes to a client, but the text was ambiguous about which OID to use and whether the server may supply concrete values such as a subjectAltName. Implementers read it differently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9908 pins down the encoding (an id-ExtensionReq attribute holding exactly one Extensions set) and adds a new CertificationRequestInfoTemplate attribute: a partly filled-in PKCS#10 request that the client completes.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now state required extensions, key types and even the subject name unambiguously, while old clients keep working. RFC 9908 updates RFC 7030 and RFC 9148 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9908 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026. It updates RFC 7030 and RFC 9148 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why the CSR Attributes Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
In RFC 7030, Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST), a client asks a server for a certificate by sending a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The server can first answer a /csrattrs request with a list of CSR Attributes, telling the client what to put in that CSR.

The trigger for this document was the Autonomic Control Plane. RFC 8994 needs every node to receive a very specific subjectAltName, and it uses /csrattrs to hand the exact value to the client. Implementation trouble showed that this use was not universally agreed upon and might even go against RFC 7030, Section 2.6. Section 4.5 of RFC 7030 was judged hard to read and ambiguous.

RFC 9908 clarifies that the server may give concrete values it demands, and extends the existing ASN.1 syntax guidance. It is described as fully backward compatible with existing use, including RFC 8994 and RFC 8995.
sections.eli5: A helper was telling people what to write on their forms, but different people understood the instructions differently. This RFC writes the instructions again so nobody is confused.

sections.title: What the Server May Ask For
sections.content:
RFC 9908 replaces the second paragraph of Section 2.6 of RFC 7030. The attributes can carry information the server cannot get itself, such as the MAC address of a client interface. The server can also give concrete values that the client is told to include, such as a specific X.509 Subject Alternative Name extension.

The attributes can also indicate the type of the public key, or which cryptographic algorithms to use for the CSR's self-signature, for example a specific elliptic curve or hash function.

The later Section 6.1 gives a privacy use: an IDevID carries a manufacturer serial number, and the server may prefer to tell the client to use a new random opaque identifier instead.
sections.eli5: The office can say "write your name here", "use this exact stamp" or "use a thick pen". It can also add details you could not know yourself.

sections.title: The Original Encoding, Made Precise
sections.content:
The ASN.1 syntax of CsrAttrs from RFC 7030, Section 4.5.2 stays unchanged, so bits on the wire remain compatible. A CsrAttrs is a sequence of AttrOrOID entries, each either a bare OID or an Attribute with a type and a set of values.

What was unclear was which OID goes in the type field and that values can hold a whole sequence of X.509 extensions. Now:

  • The type MUST be id-ExtensionReq, 1.2.840.113549.1.9.14, the same as pkcs-9-at-extensionRequest in RFC 2985. There MUST be only one such attribute.
  • Its values MUST be a set with exactly one element, of type Extensions as in RFC 5280.
  • An Extensions structure MUST NOT contain two elements with the same extnID.

To require a certain key type without the template approach, include exactly one Attribute whose type is the key-type OID, such as ecPublicKey or rsaEncryption. Its values MAY be empty, or hold parameters like an elliptic curve OID (e.g. secp384r1) or an RSA key size (e.g. 4096).
sections.eli5: The form layout did not change. What changed is the rule for which box holds the list of extra requirements, so every reader looks in the same box.

sections.title: The CSR Template Approach
sections.content:
As an alternative, RFC 9908 defines a new attribute carrying a CertificationRequestInfoTemplate: essentially a partially filled-in PKCS#10 CSR without the signature wrapper. The older template approaches in RFC 8295 and the CMP profiles (RFC 9810, RFC 9483) have drawbacks: a faked empty signature, empty strings for absent name values, and empty BIT STRINGs or OCTET STRINGs that can upset strict ASN.1 parsers.

Compared with the normal CertificationRequestInfo of RFC 5912, the template makes several parts optional:

  • subject is present only if the server has requirements on the name. An RDN with a value means the client uses that value; an RDN without a value means the client fills it in.
  • subjectPKInfo is present only if the server has requirements on the key. Its subjectPublicKey is included only to give an RSA modulus length through a placeholder key.
  • A new OID id-aa-extensionReqTemplate and an ExtensionTemplate allow an extension with its extnValue absent, meaning the client SHOULD supply a value.

The version MUST be v1 (0). The attributes MUST NOT contain more than one id-aa-extensionReqTemplate attribute, and MUST NOT contain both id-ExtensionReq and id-aa-extensionReqTemplate. Appendix A holds the full ASN.1 module.

The RFC's worked example asks for a subject with a common name left blank and two organizational unit names ("myDept" and "myGroup"), a key on curve secp256r1, a subjectAltName with a DNS entry "www.myServer.com" and an empty IP entry, a critical keyUsage and an extKeyUsage to be filled in.
sections.eli5: Instead of a list of rules, the office sends a form with some boxes already filled in and other boxes left empty. You copy it, fill the empty ones, and sign it.

sections.title: Coexistence with Existing Clients
sections.content:
Servers with legacy clients MAY keep sending the unstructured list of attribute and value pairs from RFC 7030, and MAY also include the template style for newer clients. Clients that understand both MUST use the template only and ignore all other CsrAttrs elements. Older clients simply ignore the new template element.

RFC 9908 also adds a paragraph to Section 1 of RFC 9148 (EST over CoAP): that protocol applies unchanged to RFC 7030 as updated by RFC 9908, so all references to RFC 7030 there mean the updated text.
sections.eli5: The new form and the old form can travel together. New readers use only the new form, and old readers skip the part they do not understand.

sections.title: Worked Examples of the Original Approach
sections.content:
Section 5 gives six examples, each with a plain-English explanation, the base64 DER encoding and a dumpasn1 listing. They show a subjectAltName with a specific otherName for an RFC 8994 ACP node name, the original RFC 7030 example, a specific subjectAltName extension, a public key of a specific size, a public key on a specific curve, and a mix of required extensions and attributes.

The RFC also corrects the original example in RFC 7030: its encoding of the macAddress part was not correct, because it did not follow the Extension Request attribute definition in RFC 2985. The revised encoding does not use id-ExtensionReq, since a MAC address is not an X.509 extension by itself and the server gives its OID without a value.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows several filled-in sample forms, and it also fixes a mistake in an old sample.

sections.title: Security, Identity and Privacy
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7030, Section 6 are unchanged. A separate subsection covers identity and privacy. A client may know only its Initial Device Identifier (IDevID) subject, which includes a manufacturer serial number. The server can tell the client to include a specific fully qualified domain name, to complete domain ownership proofs the CA requires.

The server may also treat the manufacturer serial number as personally identifiable information and specify a new random opaque identifier for the CSR. This can be desirable when the CA and the EST server have different operators.
sections.eli5: The office can tell you to use a made-up nickname on the form, so your real serial number is not shared around.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned the module identifier id-mod-critemplate as decimal 82 in the SMI Security for S/MIME Module Identifier registry. In the SMI Security for S/MIME Attributes registry it assigned id-aa-certificationRequestInfoTemplate as 61 and id-aa-extensionReqTemplate as 62.
sections.eli5: The number keeper wrote the new names and their numbers into the official lists.

cells: One Extensions set with unique extnIDs
One ExtensionTemplate, extnValue may be absent
